title: 5 Simple Steps for Solving Dynamic Programming Problems
beats: DP is powerful but hard; five steps, two problems (basic and harder), then general approaches
LIS defined with an example, then viewer finds LIS of a second sequence (answer 2,3,6,9 length 4)
Simplification: solve length first, sequence later
Step 1: visualize as a DAG; increasing subsequence is a path, so LIS is longest path plus one
Step 2: subproblem by fixing the endpoint; LIS ending at index k
Step 3: for index 4, read needed subproblems off the graph (idx 0,1,3), 1 + max = 3
Step 4: generalize on a second example (index 5), then the formula 1 + max over k<n with a[k]<a[n]
Step 5: solve in left-to-right order; code with list of ones, update, return max; says details don't matter
Recover the sequence itself via previous-index pointers, traced across indices 0..4
Problem 2: box stacking; two examples, pause to solve six-box case (answer 7)
Reuse the DAG: edge when box a can sit on box b; path equals a stack
Partial path equals subproblem with a box forced to be base
Relation: height of box + max over boxes that can stack on it; generalized on blue box
Ordering: sort by length or width so prerequisites come first
Code with dictionary, can_stack helper; then step through six boxes index by index
Hardest part is picking the subproblem; takes practice and creativity
Catalogue of common subproblem shapes: sequence prefix, sorted-then-prefix, two sequences, middle-out, sub-matrix
Practice is what matters; outro and Patreon

metrics.brute_force: partial 4:33: enumerates predecessors by hand per index, but no naive recursion or exponential version is shown
metrics.examples: 2 problems (LIS, box stacking) each with 2 shown inputs, then one reused example traced twice; the second problem reuses the DAG from the first
metrics.ending: catalogue of common subproblem structures plus advice to practice

theory: The video turns DP into a repeatable pipeline whose hardest step is choosing a subproblem, and it makes that step tractable by drawing a DAG so predecessors are visible. Reusing one picture across two problems builds the habit. It is weaker on discovery: the subproblem is given, not found, and naive recursion is never shown, so motivation for DP is thin.
velocity: Scene builder: render a persistent graph model and let 'needed subproblems' light up as highlighted predecessors
Playbook: pipeline of visualize, subproblem, relate, generalize, order, with a visible step tracker
Learner model: flag when learners have not seen naive recursion before DP and insert it (this video skips it)
Orchestrator: after the first problem, retrieve the same representation for the second to cut novelty cost
Evals: check that a 'common shapes' recap appears after two worked cases
quote: the hardest part is organizing the given information to identify the correct subproblem
